name: Keto Middle Eastern
summary: A week of Lebanese, Syrian, Turkish and Gulf flavours without the bread, rice or sugar: shawarma bowls, kofta, baba ghanoush, samke harra and shakshuka. Net carbs stay at 40 g or less every day, and the fat comes from olive oil, avocado, nuts, tahini and fish rather than cheese or cream.
howItWorks:
**Where the carbs went.** There is no bread, rice, bulgur or sugar here. Cauliflower stands in for the grain in tabbouleh and machboos, lettuce for the flatbread, and tomato, onion, garlic and lemon are measured like seasoning. Every day stays under the net-carb ceiling at every size.

**Fat from the pantry.** Olive oil, avocado, olives, tahini and fish carry the calories, with walnuts and hazelnuts used the way Turkish and Syrian cooks use them: in sauces, dips and fillings, over the machboos, and toasted as a snack. Labneh and yogurt are small, and lamb appears only in the weekend kofta, so saturated fat stays under 10% of calories.

**Fatty fish three times.** Anchovies on Tuesday, sardines on Friday and trout on Sunday carry the omega-3, and walnuts add a little plant omega-3 on the days between. The sardines are eaten with their soft bones, which makes Friday the big **calcium** day. Sea bass on Thursday is a fourth, leaner fish.

**Greens do the vitamin work.** Kale, spinach, romaine, arugula, parsley and cilantro turn up at almost every meal, with eggplant and cauliflower for bulk. They bring **calcium, vitamin A, folate and fibre**, a spoon of chia in the labneh plate adds more fibre, and an egg at every breakfast helps with choline.

**Cook once, eat twice.** Monday's Circassian chicken, Wednesday's stuffed eggplant, Friday's shawarma bowls and Saturday's kofta each make two portions, so the next day's lunch is done. On the Sunday before, roast the eggplant halves for Wednesday and toast a jar of hazelnuts.

recipes.name: Shakshuka with kale and parsley, and sliced avocado
recipes.inspiredBy: the shakshuka of Tunisia and Libya, now cooked all over the Levant, with kale folded into the sauce and avocado in place of the bread
recipes.about: Eggs poached in a cumin and paprika tomato sauce thick with sweet red pepper and a good handful of kale, with cool avocado on the side for the yolk. It is a favourite Middle Eastern breakfast, minus the bread, and the eggs and kale bring **choline, calcium and vitamin K** before nine in the morning.
steps: Warm the olive oil in a wide, deep frying pan over medium heat. Cook the onion and red pepper until soft, about 5 minutes.
Stir in the garlic, cumin, paprika and Aleppo pepper and cook for 30 seconds, until it smells toasty.
Add the tomato, a splash of water, the salt and the pepper. Simmer for 8 to 10 minutes, until the tomato has broken down and the sauce is thick but still saucy.
Stir in the kale and cook until it wilts and turns bright green, about 3 minutes.
Make a dip in the sauce for each egg with the back of a spoon and crack the eggs in. Cover and cook over low heat until the whites are set and the yolks are still a little wobbly, 5 to 6 minutes.
Scatter the parsley over the pan. Slice the avocado alongside and squeeze the lemon over it.
recipes.tip: Cook the tomato sauce (without the kale and eggs) in a big batch on Sunday. It keeps for 4 days, and a weekday shakshuka is then ready in 10 minutes.

recipes.name: Turkish poached egg on garlic yogurt with Aleppo pepper oil and a crisp cucumber salad
recipes.inspiredBy: Turkish çılbır, poached egg on garlicky yogurt, with olive oil in place of the butter and a cucumber salad in place of the bread
recipes.about: A soft poached egg on a cool bed of thick garlic yogurt, with a spoonful of warm olive oil blushed red with Aleppo pepper and fresh dill. A crunchy cucumber and radish salad with olives sits alongside. It is ready in 10 minutes, and the egg and thick yogurt bring **protein, choline and calcium**.
steps: Stir the yogurt with the grated garlic and a pinch of the salt. Spread it on a shallow plate and let it come to room temperature while you cook the egg.

Bring a deep pan of water to a bare simmer. Crack each egg into its own cup, swirl the water gently and slide them in one at a time. Poach for 3 minutes, until the whites are set and the yolks are runny.
Meanwhile, toss the cucumber, radish, parsley and olives with the lemon juice and the rest of the salt.
Warm the olive oil in a small pan for about 1 minute, until it shimmers, then take it off the heat and stir in the Aleppo pepper so it turns brick red.
Lift the egg (or eggs) out with a slotted spoon, blot on a towel and set on the yogurt. Spoon the hot pepper oil over, scatter with the dill and serve with the salad.
recipes.tip: No Aleppo pepper? A pinch of paprika with a pinch of chili flakes does the same job.

recipes.name: Labneh plate with a soft-boiled egg, za'atar oil, olives and cucumber
recipes.inspiredBy: the Levantine morning labneh plate, with a soft-boiled egg as on a Turkish kahvaltı table and no bread, with chia stirred through for fibre
recipes.about: A thick swoop of labneh under a pool of olive oil and za'atar, with a soft-boiled egg, peppery arugula, cool cucumber and tomato, plenty of olives and fresh mint, with a spoon of chia stirred through the labneh for a little texture. It is how a Lebanese breakfast looks, minus the bread. The egg, labneh and chia bring **choline, calcium and fibre**.
steps: Lower the egg (or eggs) into boiling water and cook for 6 minutes for a jammy yolk. Cool under cold water, then peel.

Stir the chia seeds and a spoonful of water into the labneh and let it stand for 5 minutes, so the seeds soften. (Stir it together the night before if you like it smoother.) Spread it on a plate with the back of a spoon, leaving a little dip in the middle.
Stir the za'atar into the olive oil and pour it into the dip.
Arrange the arugula, cucumber, tomato, radish and olives around it and set the egg halves on the labneh. Scatter with the mint and squeeze the lemon over the vegetables.
recipes.tip: Labneh is sold at Middle Eastern shops and many supermarkets. If you can't find it, strain thick plain yogurt in a cloth overnight.

recipes.name: Sumac beef on a bread-free fattoush with avocado
recipes.inspiredBy: Lebanese fattoush without the fried pita, with seared beef on top
recipes.about: Thin slices of seared beef over a big, sharp fattoush of romaine, kale, arugula, cucumber, tomato, radish and mint, dressed with plenty of lemon, olive oil and sumac, with creamy avocado alongside. The crunch comes from the radish and cucumber instead of fried bread. The salad is full of **vitamin C, folate and calcium**.

ingredients.note: lean round steak, sliced thin against the grain
stems removed, leaves very thinly sliced

steps: Toss the sliced beef with half the sumac, a pinch of salt and the pepper. Heat a third of the olive oil in a heavy frying pan over high heat and sear the beef in two batches, about 1 minute per side, until browned but still a little pink inside. Set aside.
For the dressing, whisk the rest of the olive oil with the lemon juice, the rest of the sumac and a pinch of salt.
Rub the kale with a spoonful of the dressing for a minute to soften it. Toss it with the romaine, arugula, cucumber, tomato, radish, parsley and mint and the rest of the dressing.
Pile the salad onto a plate and lay the beef and the avocado cubes over it.
recipes.tip: Slicing the beef very thin while it is half frozen is easiest.

recipes.name: Circassian chicken in walnut and garlic sauce, on crisp romaine
recipes.inspiredBy: Turkish çerkez tavuğu, poached chicken in a rich walnut sauce, here without the bread that usually thickens it
recipes.about: Tender poached chicken breast shredded into a creamy walnut and garlic sauce, served cool over crisp romaine with cucumber and radish and a drizzle of red paprika oil. It is a Turkish and Syrian celebration dish that eats beautifully cold, and it makes two portions. The walnuts bring **plant omega-3, copper and magnesium**.

ingredients.note: a chunk, for the poaching water

steps: Put the chicken in a pot with the onion chunk, bay leaf, a pinch of the salt and enough water to cover. Bring to a gentle simmer and poach for 14 to 16 minutes, until cooked through. Lift the chicken out and keep about 1 cup (250 ml) of the broth.

While it cooks, toast the walnuts in a dry pan for 3 minutes, until fragrant. Let them cool, then blitz them in a food processor with the garlic, lemon juice, the rest of the salt then add the warm broth a spoonful at a time until you have a thick, creamy sauce, like hummus.
Shred the chicken into thick pieces with two forks and toss it with about two thirds of the walnut sauce.
Warm the olive oil with the paprika and Aleppo pepper in a small pan for 30 seconds, until it turns a deep red.
Arrange the romaine, cucumber and radish on a plate. Pile the chicken on top, spoon over the rest of the sauce, drizzle with the red oil and scatter with the parsley and the pepper.
Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch. It is meant to be eaten cool or at room temperature, with the greens packed separately.
recipes.tip: Cooked chicken keeps well, so you can poach it on Sunday. Save the broth for soup.

recipes.name: Chicken shawarma lettuce bowls with garlic-tahini sauce, avocado and pickles
recipes.inspiredBy: Lebanese and Syrian chicken shawarma, served over crisp romaine with the pickles and garlic sauce but no flatbread
recipes.about: Thinly sliced chicken marinated in lemon, garlic and warm spices, roasted until the edges char, then piled over crunchy romaine with cucumber, tomato, pickles, avocado and a punchy garlic and tahini sauce. It makes two portions, so tomorrow's lunch is done. The chicken, tahini and parsley bring **protein, magnesium and calcium**.

ingredients.note: half for the marinade, half for the sauce

steps: Mix the sliced chicken with the olive oil, half the lemon juice, half the garlic (crushed), the baharat, cumin, turmeric, cinnamon, salt and pepper. Marinate for at least 30 minutes, or up to a day in the fridge.

Heat the oven to 230°C (450°F) and line a tray with parchment. Spread the chicken out in one layer and roast for 12 to 15 minutes, turning once, until cooked through and charred at the edges. For a more shawarma-like char, finish it for 2 minutes under the broiler.
Whisk the tahini with the rest of the garlic (crushed), the rest of the lemon and enough cold water to make a pourable sauce. It should look like thin cream. Season with a pinch of salt.
Toss the red onion with the sumac and a pinch of salt and let it sit for a few minutes to soften.
Build the bowls: romaine first, then the cucumber, tomato, pickles and parsley, then the chicken, sumac onions and sliced avocado. Spoon the sauce over.
Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch, with the sauce, the avocado and the tomato in separate containers. Reheat the chicken in a hot pan for 2 minutes and add the sauce cold.
recipes.tip: Slice the breasts thin and don't overcook them. Boneless thighs stay juicier overnight.

recipes.name: Lemon and paprika chicken şiş on cauliflower and kale tabbouleh with lemon-tahini
recipes.inspiredBy: Turkish tavuk şiş, the grilled chicken skewers, over a Lebanese-style tabbouleh with finely chopped raw cauliflower and kale in place of the bulgur
recipes.about: Juicy chicken marinated in lemon, garlic and paprika, grilled until charred at the edges and set over a bright, mostly-parsley tabbouleh with finely chopped cauliflower and kale for body and a generous ribbon of lemon-tahini. It is a fresh, sharp lunch, and the parsley, kale and cauliflower bring **vitamin C, vitamin K and calcium**.

ingredients.note: boneless, skinless breasts, cut in chunks
half for the marinade, the rest for the tabbouleh and sauce
stems removed, leaves very finely sliced

steps: Mix the chicken with the garlic, half the lemon juice, a third of the olive oil, the paprika, Aleppo pepper, cumin and half the salt. Leave it for 1 hour, or up to a day in the fridge.

Mix the cauliflower, parsley, kale, mint, cucumber and red onion in a bowl. Dress with most of the remaining lemon juice, half the remaining olive oil and the rest of the salt. Leave it for 10 minutes so the cauliflower and kale soften a little.

Thread the chicken onto skewers. Heat a grill or a heavy pan over medium-high heat with the last of the olive oil and cook the skewers for 10 to 12 minutes, turning. Pull them off the heat the moment the juices run clear.
Whisk the tahini with the last of the lemon juice and enough cold water, about 1 tablespoon, to make a pourable sauce.
Spoon the tabbouleh onto a plate, set the chicken on top and drizzle with the tahini sauce.
recipes.tip: Cut the cauliflower by pulsing it in a food processor, a few short bursts, so it doesn't turn to mush. For a packed lunch, grill the skewers the night before and keep the tahini sauce separate.

recipes.name: Beef-stuffed eggplant with tomato, peppers and lemony kale
recipes.inspiredBy: Turkish karnıyarık, the "split belly" eggplant stuffed with spiced beef, tomato and pepper, with walnuts in the filling as in a Turkish içli köfte, and garlicky greens in place of the pilaf
recipes.about: Silky roasted eggplant halves split open and filled with a savoury beef, onion, tomato and pepper mixture with toasted walnuts, baked in a little tomato sauce and served with a pile of garlicky sautéed kale. It is a classic Turkish family dish, and it makes two portions, so tomorrow's lunch is ready. The eggplant and kale bring **fibre, calcium and potassium**.

ingredients.note: lean round steak, minced by the butcher or ground in a food processor
1 small, slim eggplant per person (Japanese or Italian), halved lengthwise
diced, with a thin slice kept back for each eggplant half

steps: Heat the oven to 220°C (425°F). Score the cut side of each eggplant half in a crisscross, brush with about a third of the olive oil and season with salt. Roast cut side up on a lined tray for 25 minutes, until soft and golden.
Meanwhile, toast the walnuts in a dry pan until fragrant, about 3 minutes, and set them aside.
Warm half the remaining olive oil in a large pan and cook the onion and red pepper until soft, about 6 minutes. Add half the garlic, then the beef, and break it up. Brown it well, about 7 minutes.
Stir in the tomato paste, paprika, Aleppo pepper, diced tomato, pepper and a splash of water. Simmer for 5 to 6 minutes, until thick. Stir in the parsley, walnuts and half the lemon juice.

Press the middle of each roasted eggplant half down with a spoon to make a boat. Mound in as much filling as the boats will hold and spoon the rest around them, top each with a slice of tomato and pour about 1/4 cup (60 ml) of water into the tray around them.
Bake for 20 minutes, until the eggplant is meltingly soft and the tops are lightly browned.

While it bakes, warm the last of the olive oil in a wide pan, add the rest of the garlic, sliced, and stir for 30 seconds. Add the kale with a splash of water and a pinch of salt, cover and cook for 5 minutes, until tender. Finish with the rest of the lemon juice.
Serve two eggplant halves and their filling per person with the kale. Keep the second for tomorrow's lunch; it reheats well and keeps for 3 days.
recipes.tip: Salting the eggplant isn't necessary. Roasting it face up gives it the soft, sweet texture without extra oil. Roast the eggplant halves on Sunday and the filling comes together in 25 minutes.

recipes.name: Gulf-style grilled sea bass with spiced cauliflower rice and dakkous
recipes.inspiredBy: Gulf grilled fish with baharat, machboos-style spiced rice made from cauliflower, and the tomato-garlic chili sauce called dakkous, finished with toasted nuts the way machboos is
recipes.about: Sea bass fillets rubbed with baharat and lemon, grilled until the skin crisps, over cauliflower cooked with cardamom, cinnamon, turmeric and loomi in the style of a machboos, with wilted spinach, toasted hazelnuts and a hot, garlicky tomato dakkous. The fish, cauliflower and spinach bring **selenium, vitamin C and folate**.

ingredients.note: half for the fish, half for the dakkous
ground, or a pinch of crushed dried lime

steps: Toast the hazelnuts in a dry pan for 3 minutes, until golden, and chop them roughly. Mix a third of the olive oil with half the lemon juice, half the garlic (crushed), the baharat, a pinch of salt and the pepper. Rub it over the fish and leave it for 15 minutes.

Make the dakkous. Chop the tomato, serrano, the rest of the garlic and the cilantro very finely together on a board, or pound them in a mortar, then stir in the cumin, the rest of the lemon juice and a pinch of salt. It should be a coarse, juicy sauce.
Warm half the remaining olive oil in a wide pan and cook the onion until soft, about 4 minutes. Add the cardamom, cinnamon, turmeric and loomi and stir for 20 seconds.
Add the cauliflower and a pinch of salt. Cook, stirring, for 5 to 6 minutes, until just tender but with a little bite. Add the spinach and cook for 1 minute more, until it wilts.
Heat a grill pan, a heavy frying pan or the grill to high. Cook the fish skin side down for 4 to 5 minutes without moving it, until the skin is crisp, then flip for 1 to 2 minutes more.
Serve the fish over the cauliflower rice, scattered with the hazelnuts, with the dakkous, and a small salad of arugula and cucumber dressed with the last of the olive oil and a pinch of salt.
recipes.tip: Any firm white fish works: sea bream, snapper or haddock fillets cook the same way.

recipes.name: Pan-seared fresh anchovies with sumac onions and a parsley, radish and kale salad
recipes.inspiredBy: Turkish hamsi tava, the fresh Black Sea anchovies cooked in a hot pan, with a Levantine sumac onion salad and no cornmeal coating, and the walnut and hazelnut tarator Turkish fish restaurants serve with fried fish
recipes.about: Whole fresh anchovies seared in a hot pan until the skins crackle, over a sharp salad of parsley, radish, kale and arugula with thin sumac onions, lemon and a spoonful of rough walnut and hazelnut tarator. Anchovies are the little oily fish people fry all along the Turkish coast. A serving carries **omega-3, calcium and selenium**.

ingredients.note: half for the salad, the rest to squeeze over the fish
stems removed, leaves very thinly sliced

steps: Toast the walnuts and hazelnuts in a dry pan for 3 minutes. Pound them in a mortar, or blitz them in a mini chopper, with a little of the garlic, a squeeze of the lemon, a pinch of salt and a splash of water, into a rough, creamy tarator.
Toss the red onion with the sumac and a pinch of salt and leave it for 5 minutes to soften.
Rub the kale with a pinch of salt and half the garlic for a minute to soften it. Toss it with the parsley, radish, cucumber and arugula, the onions, half the lemon juice and a third of the olive oil.
Pat the anchovies very dry and season them with salt, pepper and the rest of the garlic. Heat the rest of the olive oil in a large non-stick pan over high heat.

Lay the anchovies in the pan in a single layer, in two batches if you need to, and cook for 2 minutes without moving them, until the skins are crisp. Flip and cook for 1 minute more, until just opaque.
Pile the salad on a plate and set the anchovies on top. Spoon the tarator alongside, squeeze over the rest of the lemon and finish with the Aleppo pepper.
recipes.tip: Fresh sardines are easier to find in North America and work the same way: scale and gut them, or ask the fishmonger, and cook 2 to 3 minutes a side. Smelt and small mackerel fillets also work.

recipes.name: Sardine, tomato and parsley salad with avocado and lemon-tahini
recipes.inspiredBy: Lebanese-style canned sardines with tomato, parsley and lemon, with avocado and a tahini dressing added
recipes.about: Canned sardines, soft bones and all, flaked over a bright salad of ripe tomato, cucumber, a big handful of parsley and creamy avocado, with lemon-tahini poured over. It takes 10 minutes and nothing gets cooked. The sardines bring **calcium, omega-3 and vitamin B12**.

ingredients.note: canned in water or brine, drained, bones in
half for the salad, half for the dressing

steps: Toss the red onion with the sumac and a pinch of salt and leave it for 5 minutes.
Whisk the tahini with the crushed garlic, half the lemon juice and cold water, a teaspoon at a time until pourable.
Toss the romaine, tomato, cucumber, parsley and mint with the olive oil, the rest of the lemon juice, the onions and a pinch of salt and pepper.
Pile the salad onto a plate. Flake the sardines over it in big pieces and add the avocado.
Drizzle the tahini dressing over everything and eat right away.
recipes.tip: Buy sardines packed in water or brine, not oil, for a fresher taste. Drain them but keep the soft bones: that is where the calcium is.

recipes.name: Lamb and beef kofta platter with baba ghanoush, charred pepper and a sumac arugula salad
recipes.inspiredBy: Lebanese kafta mashwiyye, the grilled lamb and beef skewers with parsley, served mezze-style with smoky baba ghanoush
recipes.about: Juicy lamb and beef skewers with parsley, scented with baharat and cinnamon, grilled and served on a platter with smoky baba ghanoush, a charred red pepper, a sharp arugula salad with parsley and sumac, and a walnut and tahini tarator. It is the weekend project, and it makes two portions. The meat brings **zinc and iron**, and the eggplant adds potassium and fibre.

ingredients.note: lean leg, ground twice or minced by the butcher
lean round, ground or minced by the butcher
finely chopped, two thirds for the kofta
a third for the baba ghanoush, the rest for the sauce
toasted and finely chopped, for the sauce
for the baba ghanoush, the sauce and the salad
one wide strip, about a quarter of a pepper, for charring

steps: Prick the eggplant and char it directly over a gas flame, under a very hot broiler or on the grill for 15 to 20 minutes, turning, until the skin is blackened and the flesh is collapsing. Set it in a bowl and cover it for 10 minutes.

Scoop the soft flesh out, drain off any bitter liquid, and mash it with a third of the tahini, a third of the lemon juice, a little garlic, a drizzle of the olive oil and a pinch of salt. It should be smoky and slightly rough.

Make the kofta mixture. Knead the lamb and beef with the onion, two thirds of the parsley, a spoonful of the olive oil, the baharat, the cinnamon, the salt and the pepper for a full minute, until sticky and well combined. Shape it into long, flat fingers around skewers, or into short ovals if you are using a pan.

Brush the kofta and the pepper strip with some of the olive oil. Grill, broil or pan-sear the kofta for 8 to 10 minutes, turning, until browned and just cooked through. Char the pepper skin side down until blistered, then slice it.

Toast the walnuts in a dry pan for 3 minutes. Whisk the rest of the tahini with the rest of the garlic, half the remaining lemon juice, the walnuts and about 2 tablespoons of cold water into a pourable tarator.
Toss the arugula with the rest of the parsley, the sumac, the last of the lemon juice and a drizzle of the remaining olive oil.
Serve the kofta on a platter with the baba ghanoush, pepper, tomato slices and salad, with the tarator spooned over. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch.
recipes.tip: Lean lamb can go dry, so don't skip the grated onion, and take the kofta off as soon as they are just cooked through. Reheat leftover kofta in a hot pan for 2 minutes.

recipes.name: Baked whole trout with a cilantro, walnut and chili sauce, and garlicky kale
recipes.inspiredBy: Lebanese samke harra, the baked fish with a spicy cilantro and nut sauce, made with a whole trout and served with Black Sea style sautéed kale
recipes.about: A whole trout stuffed with parsley and baked until the skin crisps, under a hot, green sauce of cilantro, garlic, chili, walnuts and lemon, with a pile of garlicky sautéed kale. It is simple enough for a weekend dinner and good enough to be a feast. The trout and walnuts bring **omega-3, B12 and copper**, and the kale adds calcium and vitamin A.

ingredients.note: 1 whole trout, cleaned; buy a fish about half as heavy again as the weight shown
about half for the sauce, the rest for the fish and kale
a few sprigs for the fish

steps: Heat the oven to 220°C (425°F). Pat the trout dry and make 3 shallow slashes on each side. Rub the skin and the inside with a little of the olive oil, salt and pepper, and tuck the parsley sprigs into the cavity.
Lay the trout on a lined tray and roast it for 18 to 22 minutes, until the flesh flakes at the thickest part and the skin is crisp.

While it bakes, make the sauce. Blitz the walnuts with the cilantro, most of the garlic, the serrano, half the lemon juice, half the remaining olive oil and a pinch of salt, adding a few tablespoons of water, until you have a thick, spoonable sauce.

Warm the rest of the olive oil in a wide pan over medium heat and add the last of the garlic, sliced. Stir for 30 seconds, then add the kale with a splash of water and a pinch of salt. Cover and cook for 5 to 6 minutes, until tender.

Lift the trout onto a platter, spoon the sauce over and around it, and squeeze over a little of the remaining lemon juice. Dress the kale with the rest of the lemon and the sumac and serve it alongside.
recipes.tip: A whole trout gives about two thirds of its weight as fish. Ask the fishmonger to gut and scale it; fillets work too, roasted for 10 to 12 minutes.

recipes.name: Toasted hazelnuts with Aleppo pepper and lemon
recipes.inspiredBy: the warm, salted hazelnuts sold in Turkish nut shops (çerez), from the Black Sea hazelnut groves
recipes.about: A warm handful of hazelnuts toasted in a dry pan with a little Aleppo pepper, a squeeze of lemon and salt, the way a Turkish nut shop sells them. They are sweet, crunchy and a little hot, and bring **vitamin E, magnesium and healthy fat** with almost no carbs.
steps: Heat a small dry pan over medium heat. Add the hazelnuts and toast, shaking the pan, until they smell nutty and the skins crackle, about 4 minutes.
Tip them into a bowl, rub off any loose skins with a towel if you like, and toss with the Aleppo pepper, lemon juice and salt while they are warm.
recipes.tip: Toast a big batch on Sunday and keep it in a jar for the week.

recipes.name: Muhammara with cucumber and radish
recipes.inspiredBy: Syrian muhammara from Aleppo, the roasted red pepper and walnut dip, made without the breadcrumbs and pomegranate molasses
recipes.about: A rich, smoky, slightly hot dip of roasted red pepper and walnuts with a squeeze of lemon, scooped up with cucumber and radish. The walnuts bring **plant omega-3**, and the pepper brings vitamin C.
steps: Use a jarred roasted red pepper, drained and rinsed, or roast a whole pepper under a hot broiler or over a flame until blackened all over, about 15 minutes. Let it steam in a covered bowl, then peel off the skin and remove the seeds.
Toast the walnuts in a dry pan for 2 minutes, until fragrant.
Blitz the pepper, walnuts, olive oil, lemon juice, garlic, Aleppo pepper, cumin and salt to a thick, slightly coarse paste.
Spoon into a bowl and serve with the cucumber and radish.
recipes.tip: It keeps for 5 days in the fridge, so make a double batch.

recipes.name: Warm za'atar olives
recipes.inspiredBy: Lebanese and Palestinian olives warmed with za'atar and olive oil
recipes.about: Rinsed black olives warmed in olive oil with a little za'atar and lemon. It is salty, herby and very satisfying, and the olives bring **vitamin E and healthy fat** with almost no carbs.
steps: Rinse the olives under cold water and pat them dry.
Warm the olive oil in a small pan over low heat. Add the olives and the za'atar and stir for 2 minutes, until warm and fragrant.
Squeeze the lemon over everything and eat warm.
recipes.tip: Rinsing cuts the salt on olives noticeably. Leave the pits in for the best flavour, and watch your teeth.

recipes.name: Avocado with lemon, za'atar and olive oil
recipes.inspiredBy: the way labneh is dressed on a Levantine breakfast table, with olive oil, lemon and za'atar, here on avocado
recipes.about: A whole ripe avocado, halved, with a squeeze of lemon, a drizzle of olive oil and a good shake of za'atar. It takes a minute, and the avocado brings **potassium, folate and fibre**.
steps: Halve the avocado and remove the stone.
Squeeze the lemon over the cut face, drizzle with the olive oil and sprinkle with the za'atar and a tiny pinch of salt.
Eat it with a spoon, straight from the skin.
recipes.tip: Pick the avocado a couple of days ahead. It should give slightly when pressed.

recipes.name: Spiced hazelnuts and walnuts with sumac and Aleppo pepper
recipes.inspiredBy: the mixed roasted nuts sold across the Gulf and the Levant, with the Black Sea hazelnuts and the walnuts of the Syrian and Turkish kitchen
recipes.about: Hazelnuts and walnuts toasted in a dry pan with sumac, Aleppo pepper and a little salt. It is a crunchy, tangy little handful that brings **vitamin E, plant omega-3 and magnesium**.
steps: Toast the hazelnuts and walnuts in a dry pan over medium heat, shaking now and then, until they smell nutty, about 3 minutes.
Toss with the olive oil, sumac, Aleppo pepper and salt while they are warm.
recipes.tip: Make extra and keep it in a jar for up to a week.

recipes.name: Olive oil artichoke hearts with dill, lemon and toasted hazelnuts
recipes.inspiredBy: Turkish zeytinyağlı enginar, the cold artichoke hearts dressed with olive oil, lemon and dill
recipes.about: Tender artichoke hearts dressed with olive oil, lemon and fresh dill, with toasted hazelnuts for crunch. It is a classic Turkish cold meze that takes five minutes from a jar, and the artichokes bring **fibre and folate** for very few carbs.

ingredients.note: hearts in brine, drained and rinsed

steps: Toast the hazelnuts in a dry pan over medium heat until golden, about 3 minutes. Tip them out to cool, then chop them roughly.
Drain the artichoke hearts, rinse them well and pat them dry. Halve them if they are large.
Toss them with the olive oil, lemon juice, dill, Aleppo pepper and a tiny pinch of salt.
Pile onto a plate and scatter the hazelnuts over the top.
recipes.tip: Choose artichoke hearts packed in brine or water rather than oil, and rinse them.

recipes.name: Avocado with lemon-tahini, sumac and radish
recipes.inspiredBy: the lemon-tahini and sumac that dress hummus on a Levantine table, here spooned over avocado
recipes.about: A small ripe avocado, halved, with a ribbon of lemon-tahini, a dusting of sumac, thin radish and a little cilantro. It is creamy and tangy, and the avocado and tahini bring **fibre, potassium and calcium**.

ingredients.note: about 1 small avocado, halved and pitted

steps: Whisk the tahini with the lemon juice, a pinch of the salt and enough cold water, about 1 tablespoon, to make a pourable sauce.
Set the avocado halves on a plate and spoon the sauce into and over them.
Top with the radish and cilantro and finish with the sumac.
recipes.tip: Pick the avocado a couple of days ahead. It should give slightly when pressed.

recipes.name: Roasted pumpkin seeds with sumac and Aleppo pepper
recipes.inspiredBy: the salted roasted seeds sold at every nut shop in Lebanon, Syria and Turkey, eaten by the handful
recipes.about: Pumpkin seeds toasted in a dry pan with sumac, Aleppo pepper and a pinch of salt until they pop and turn golden. They are crunchy, tangy and a little hot, and bring **zinc, magnesium and iron**.
steps: Toast the pumpkin seeds in a dry pan over medium heat, stirring, until they puff and turn golden, about 4 minutes.
Toss with the olive oil, sumac, Aleppo pepper and salt while they are warm.
recipes.tip: They keep for 2 weeks in a jar, so toast a bigger batch if you like them.

recipes.name: Olive and walnut dip with crisp romaine
recipes.inspiredBy: the olive and walnut pastes of Hatay and Gaziantep, served as a meze with raw vegetables
recipes.about: A coarse, garlicky paste of rinsed olives, toasted walnuts, parsley and lemon, scooped up with crisp romaine leaves. It is salty, nutty and bright, and the walnuts bring **plant omega-3 and copper**.
steps: Toast the walnuts in a dry pan for 2 to 3 minutes, until fragrant.
Pulse the olives, walnuts, garlic, lemon juice, olive oil and parsley in a small processor to a coarse paste, adding a spoonful of water if it is stiff.
Spoon into a bowl, sprinkle with the Aleppo pepper and serve with the romaine leaves for scooping.
recipes.tip: It keeps for 4 days in a jar in the fridge.
